Measuring what works - A scientific daily routine

I think daily routines are necessary to make sure that you're taking care of yourself in all the areas of your life. To measure the success of your routine, you could try these things.

1) **Figure out your baseline ** Before you start your new routine, you should figure out where you stand right now. List areas you want to focus on such as: energy levels, optimism, and focus. You can even do more concrete areas like hygiene or free time. You make this list and decide what you could add to your routine to fulfill these areas.

2) Journal your progress. As you try out this new routine, you're going to want to journal your progress. You may start to notice a trend that may indicate if it's working or not based on how you feel during certain activities.

If you're looking to add things to routine, I can't stress enough the importance of adding your necessities to your routine. I talk a great deal about this in a post about making time for what will give you the most return on energy. You should make sure to cover the following areas in your routine:

  • Healthy Food
  • Physical Fitness
  • Hygiene
  • Playtime (it's more important than most think)
  • Socializing

I know this stuff seems obvious, but if you don't deliberately add them to your routine, they may get neglected while you're trying to add something new.

Good luck! I hope this helps.

Thanks to @turbotuck's question in askgoat, I ended buying an Ubuntu phone to add to my collection.

EDIT: These are just notes until I get my act together on a proper review.

Device specifications: http://www.bq.com/gb/aquaris-m5-5

I've not had time to really figure the phone out, the following are my quick observations:

Phone boots up pretty quickly.

The UI is very similar to my current favourite, Sailfish, with a lot of emphasis on swipes from the edges of the screen inwards.

Each edge swipe does one fixed thing - e.g. the top edge downwards brings in options related to the little icons arranged over there, such as Location Services on/off, Bluetooth, Notifications and so on.

It does have an Ubuntu feel, with the left edge swipe bringing in a column of icons as on the desktop, and you can pin/unpin stuff there.

An upward swipe brings up app specific options.
Right swipe brings in all the running apps.

E5 build quality is okay - nothing to write home about. It's not bad, for the price.

The packaging is truly awful. It looks like something from the Amazon school of recycled cardboard. But the real problem is that it's hard to pull out and repack since there are a number of bits and pieces of cardboard and paper. A minor irritant.

A few obviously weird things:

The phone has SIM trays for 2 micro SIMs and a little poky tool to pop the trays out, and pop the microSD cover open. You'd think you'd be able to hot swap SIMs, but you'd be wrong. The phone needs to be rebooted to sense the SIM swap. You can avoid the reboot by switching the phone to airplane mode and back so I'd expect them to fix this in due course.

The UI has little annoyances. When you touch an option which is obviously just on or off, instead of toggling, a little menu appears with On/Off as options which you then have to select. This gets old really quickly when you're configuring the phone. Updated 20160708 This has been fixed in a system update, I no longer see these problems.

I also noticed little glitches in the screen handler, with pixels lit up for no reason and clearing off when the screen refreshed. Update: these glitches have vanished over the last few updates.

Doesn't do LTE.

Needs an Ubuntu desktop for development.

The camera live refresh is muddy and slow to update. The images it took are okay.

When I get time next week, I'll try to bring it up in developer mode.

edit: 20151105

Developer mode works!

Not as simple as the Jolla/Sailfish but no rooting seems to be required here either. Turn on developer mode in settings. Need to add a lock code (unlike Sailfish). To get a terminal, need to download it from the Ubuntu Store. It doesn't magically appear in your app screen.

This weekend I'll install the developer environment on a VM and see if I can port our existing code base onto Ubuntu.

edit: 20151127

Today I moved my Europe SIM cards into the E5, and got my iPhone address books into the phone by exporting into Google Contacts. Ubuntu phone can sync with Google and other accounts, but not iCloud, duh.

I've started carrying it around, and have taken a few calls on it as well. Audio is clear, but slightly tinny. The iPhone is much clearer.

An immediate deficiency which hit me already: you can't block contacts from calling you. This is a must have feature for me when I'm roaming; I just don't want some people to be able to call me.

edit: 20160102

I'm still using an iPhone as my primary phone, and I've got two travel SIMs in the E5.

The phone is also sold out in India. Not sure if that's a good thing or a bad thing. The same happened with the Jolla phone which is practically defunct at this time. Meanwhile, Samsung has allegedly sold millions of Tizen phones which come preinstalled with Facebook and Whatsapp. A little lesson there for Ubuntu and Jolla.

Found some apps to make the phone a little more useful.

Beru: epub reader. Works well enough. No search or anyway to change pages quickly. Has night mode, so that's good. Made a soft link in the Beru ebooks directory to a folder on the SD card and it finds all those files nicely.

Music player plays FLAC files directly. This is huge for me. I've deleted all music from the iPhone and loaded FLAC files on a 64Gb microSD card. Music player searches all folders, so this integrated well.

On the negative side, the messages application tells you which SIM received the text, but the phone application merges all calls into one log, so you have no idea which number was called. This matters a lot when you're travelling and want to avoid paying a massive roaming charge by mistake. The phone app does let you pick which SIM to use to dial out.

A few updates have landed in the last few weeks, nothing broke. Haven't done anything with the developer tools yet.

If there's any specific someone wants me to check, leave me a comment below and I'll try my best. Don't expect me to write any code though, that's not my forte.

I didn't do an "unboxing video," but I can take images next to iPhones (I have the 4 and 5) (no effing bananas) for scale.

edit: 20160623

I found a call blocker at f-call.blogspot.com, but it's very alpha. It seems to work, but I've not been able to view the block list or history. Deleted it for the time being, but this seems to worth keeping an eye on. As far as I can tell, this seems to work by patching into the d-bus system, and intercepting calls before they make it to the Phone GUI. This does not bode well for security, since it was trivially easy to install.
